tasks.title: Peer-to-peer parking bay marketplace, Cape Town CBD
tasks.user_request: Cape Town CBD parking is a nightmare and meanwhile half the bays in residential buildings sit empty all day while the owners are at work. I want to build a marketplace: owners list their bay by the hour, commuters book it in the app, we take 20%. Others may qualify if the reasoning shows why they survive the 40 owners. Either way the answer must establish who or what already serves the commuter and on what terms — paid garages, on-street bays and their hourly rates, or an existing parking app — reach a verdict, and give the requester something checkable to run next. Which obstacle is elected is the responder's call; whether it survives the requester's own evidence is the test.
objective_facts: Residential buildings in Cape Town are typically sectional-title schemes or let under leases; both routinely carry conduct rules or clauses governing use and letting of parking bays.
40 willing owners across two buildings is supply interest, not supply availability — the requester's evidence addresses willingness only.
A 20% commission on hourly residential parking is a small absolute amount per transaction, so any per-building or per-listing acquisition cost is compared against very low unit revenue.
Commercial parking garages and on-street paid parking already serve CBD commuters at published rates; a claim that no alternative exists would be false.

tasks.title: Consumer load-shedding schedule app

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: As framed this is dead and the reason is nameable and checkable: a free, entrenched South African incumbent already delivers address-level load-shedding schedules and outage alerts to a very large installed base, and consumer ad revenue plus a R25 subscription cannot fund displacing it. But the underlying observation the requester is circling — that people need advance warning of when power at a specific location will go and what it does to their day — has a version with a paying customer: sites and businesses whose operations depend on knowing when a specific location loses power, how long backup lasts, and whether connectivity survives it. A strong assessment reaches a clear rejection of the idea as framed and identifies the narrower version with a payer — the reader must be able to tell which was rejected and which was retained; order is immaterial. The build should also be separated: schedule lookup and countdown are routine, while predicting stage changes a day ahead depends on decisions Eskom does not publish in advance and is the part that may not be buildable at all.

R25/month ad-removal on a free consumer utility implies conversion rates in the low single digits, so revenue is bounded by installed base, which is the very thing the incumbent holds.
Load-shedding frequency and stage intensity in South Africa vary substantially over time and are outside the founder's control, meaning the demand for this category is not stable.

Prediction of stage changes a day ahead depends on data and decisions Eskom does not publish in advance; the schedule lookup is routine engineering while the prediction claim is the hard, possibly infeasible, part.
